## Context

In order to create any workloads in K8s, an image has to exist on the node or be pulled in from an OCI Distribution server (docker registry). Local K8s distros such as KIND, K3D, K3S, Microk8s have CLI support for injecting or pushing images into the CRIs of cluster nodes. No standard or tool exists to do this generically in K8s as the CRI sits outside the problem of K8s beyond just communicating with it. For Zarf to push images into a K8s cluster that does not have a CLI option to inject the image, we have to establish some mechanism to create a temporary registry, use an existing one, or inject the image in the cluster. Zarf must also support unknown environments with no other dependencies; we cannot assume a registry exists. Typically when K8s pulls images from a remote registry, it sends the request to the CRI that then does the pull outside of the K8s context. The CRI runs at the host level on a per-node basis, so to access a private registry, the TLS trust needs to be modified on any host/node that would attempt to pull the image. The two primary ways to do this are modifying the node's root certificate authorities or the CRIs configuration if it has an option for TLS root CA. Lastly, as this is per node, all nodes in the cluster would need to be modified or some affinity/taint to force the pod to use a single node during bootstrapping.

# Architectural Decision Record: Container Image Distribution in Zarf

## Decision

Zarf shall implement a **multi-strategy image injection system** comprising:

1. **Primary Strategy**: Deploy a temporary in-cluster registry (containerized) as a bootstrap service that:
   - Runs on a single node during initialization
   - Accepts pushed images from the Zarf CLI
   - Serves images to cluster workloads via internal networking
   - Is automatically removed post-deployment

2. **Secondary Strategy**: Support external/existing registry integration where available with automatic TLS trust configuration

3. **Fallback Strategy**: Direct node-level CRI image injection for local K8s distros with CLI support

## Rationale

- **Eliminates external dependencies**: Works in air-gapped/unknown environments without assuming registry availability
- **Minimizes node modifications**: Temporary registry approach avoids permanent host-level TLS configuration changes
- **Scales across multi-node clusters**: Registry runs in-cluster, accessible to all nodes via internal networking; avoids per-node TLS modification complexity
- **Supports diverse environments**: Prioritizes local distro CLI support where available, falls back to temporary registry for standard K8s clusters
- **Reversible**: Bootstrap registry lifecycle is controlled and cleaned up automatically

## Consequences

**Positive:**
- Operator convenience: Single mechanism works across cluster types
- Security: No persistent host-level TLS modifications needed
- Testability: Temporary registry can be validated before production workload deployment

**Negative:**
- Additional complexity in bootstrap phase
- Temporary registry consumes cluster resources during initialization
- Network performance dependency for image pulling

## Implementation Considerations

- Auto-detect local K8s distro capabilities and use native CLI when available
- Implement health checks and retry logic for image injection
- Document registry timeout and resource limits
- Provide observability into image pull status during bootstrap

## Decision

Because we cannot require third-party dependencies, the requirement from some cloud-managed or distro-managed registry is not an option as not every K8s cluster will have that available.  Running an in-memory registry while zarf is performing `zarf init` was initially explored to resolve the external dependency issue.  However, this solution proved too complex when dealing with network traversal (especially behind NATs), firewall, and NACL rulesets.  Additionally, because of the complexities around TLS trust, the in-memory registry was not a viable solution.

After iterating on several solutions, including `kubectl cp`, `kubectl exec`, a busybox configmap injection that brought in netcat to stream files, and a few variations on those ideas, we found using only configmaps to be the most predictable method for injection. The challenge with this mode is that the ETCD limit is 1 MB total, with binary data base64-encoded leaving roughly 670 KBs of data per configmap, far too small to bring the registry tarball in a single configmap. So instead, we used a combination of a custom Rust binary compiled with MUSL to perform file concatenation, untarring, and verification of a set of split tarball chunks across a variable number of configmaps. We found that chunking by less than the near-maximum configmap size was more performant on some resource-constrained control planes. The details of this solution and a drawing are located in the main README of this repo.

Accepted

- **Validation**: Include SBOM accuracy in release checklist

# Architectural Decision Record: Zarf Image and Secret Mutation Strategy

## Status
Proposed

## Context

Zarf currently uses Helm Post Rendering to mutate image paths and secrets for integration with the internal Zarf Registry. This approach has limitations:

1. **GitOps Tool Incompatibility**: When using secondary GitOps tools (Flux, ArgoCD, etc.), Zarf cannot perform mutations since it no longer controls manifest application
2. **CRD Git Server References**: Custom Resources that reference the Zarf Git Server are not being mutated properly
3. **Package Author Burden**: Authors must manually implement rudimentary templating and use `zarf prepare` commands
4. **Scalability Issues**: The current approach doesn't scale well beyond simple Kubernetes deployments

## Decision

Implement a **declarative mutation framework** that decouples image/secret mutation from Helm rendering and GitOps tool execution.

### Key Components:

1. **Mutation Specification Layer**: Define a standardized format for declaring mutation rules within Zarf packages that is tool-agnostic
2. **Pre-Package Processing**: Generate fully mutated manifests during package creation rather than at deployment time
3. **Zarf Injector**: Deploy a lightweight mutating webhook that applies mutations at runtime for GitOps-managed resources
4. **Package Metadata**: Embed mutation rules as package metadata that tooling can consume

## Rationale

- **Shifts responsibility appropriately**: Zarf (not package authors) determines mutation logic
- **GitOps Compatible**: Mutations are applied via admission controller, compatible with all GitOps tools
- **Future-Proof**: Extensible framework supports additional mutation types beyond images/secrets
- **Reduced Friction**: Eliminates need for `zarf prepare` and manual templating

## Consequences

**Positive:**
- Single source of truth for mutation rules
- Works with any deployment mechanism
- Reduced package author cognitive load
- Improved GitOps integration

**Negative:**
- Additional webhook infrastructure required
- Increased complexity in mutation framework
- Requires migration path for existing packages

# ADR: Simplify Registry Initialization by Removing stage2 Binary

## Status
Proposed

## Context

ADR 3 introduced a two-stage approach using:
- `stage1`: Rust binary that re-assembles a `registry:2` image from configmaps
- `stage2`: Go binary that performs three sequential operations:
  1. Start docker registry in read-write mode
  2. Push the `registry:2` crane tarball into the registry
  3. Restart docker registry in read-only mode

The `registry:2` image is immediately consumed by the `zarf-registry` package to create an in-cluster registry, after which the injector pod is destroyed.

## Problem

The current two-stage approach introduces unnecessary operational overhead:
- **Maintenance burden**: Three binaries to track and maintain in the Zarf ecosystem
- **Configuration bloat**: Nearly doubled configmaps loaded during cluster initialization (performance impact)
- **Build complexity**: Cross-platform compilation required for each release (increased build time and CI complexity)
- **Resource inefficiency**: Full-featured docker registry used as temporary intermediary for a single image

## Decision

Remove the `stage2` binary and consolidate registry initialization into `stage1`. The Rust binary will directly handle all three registry operations, eliminating the intermediate bootstrap registry.

**Alternative approaches considered:**
- Replace both binaries with a shell script wrapper (less robust, harder to maintain)
- Keep current architecture (rejected due to overhead concerns)
- Use a lighter container image (does not address the design complexity)

## Consequences

### Positive
- Reduces operational complexity by eliminating one binary
- Decreases cluster initialization time and memory overhead (fewer configmaps)
- Simplifies build pipeline and CI/CD (single cross-platform compilation)
- Improves resource efficiency during cluster bootstrap
- Easier to maintain and troubleshoot the bootstrap process

### Negative
- Increases `stage1` Rust binary complexity slightly
- Requires careful handling of docker registry lifecycle in Rust
- Testing must cover registry state transitions

## Implications

- Update build toolchain to remove stage2 compilation
- Refactor `stage1` to include docker registry lifecycle management
- Update documentation and deployment procedures
- Simplify configmap generation and injection logic

# Architectural Decision Record: Testing Strategy Enhancement for Zarf

## Decision

**Adopt Option 2: Introduce Unit Testing in a defined and limited capacity within Zarf**

## Rationale

This option provides the optimal balance between addressing the identified gaps and maintaining pragmatic governance:

### Why This Over Alternatives

**vs. Option 1 (Comprehensive Unit Testing):**
- Avoids the "test decay" problem where unit tests become brittle as code evolves
- Prevents tests from being written to implementation details rather than behavior
- Reduces long-term maintenance burden while still improving coverage

**vs. Option 3 (Integration/Partial E2E Testing):**
- Simpler to implement and maintain than complex orchestration layers
- More practical for library interface validation
- Directly targets the stated pain point: untestable code sections

### Strategic Benefits

1. **Library Interface Protection** - Unit tests on public APIs ensure contract stability as Zarf becomes a library
2. **Focused Coverage** - Targets only hard-to-test areas (utilities, business logic, configuration parsing) rather than attempting comprehensive coverage
3. **Sustainable Model** - Lower maintenance overhead increases adoption and code review compliance

## Implementation Guidelines

### Scope Definition
- Unit tests required for: utility functions, configuration handlers, data validators, error handling logic
- Unit tests optional for: UI layers, external integrations, simple CRUD operations
- Unit tests forbidden in: code that duplicates e2e test coverage

### Quality Gates
- Establish clear patterns/examples for acceptable unit tests
- Require code review verification that tests validate *behavior*, not implementation
- Periodically audit tests for specification drift

### Governance
- Create a TESTING.md guide with decision trees for "should this be unit tested?"
- Establish team review process specifically for unit test PRs to maintain standards

## Risks Mitigated
- **Test maintenance burden**: Limited scope prevents sprawl
- **Library stability**: Public interfaces gain test-backed guarantees
- **E2E redundancy**: Clear boundaries prevent duplicate testing

# Architectural Decision Record: SBOM Generation for Non-Image Dependencies

## Decision

**Implement Option 2: Run Syft against files and dataInjections, with a clear documentation path for users to extend SBOM coverage as needed.**

### Why Not Option 1
- The noise-to-signal ratio is too high; git repository metadata and transitive dependencies would create SBOMs of questionable value
- Users would struggle to distinguish between actual package contents and build artifacts
- Maintenance burden would increase with false-positive vulnerability reports

- Optional complexity features tend to remain unused and poorly documented

1. **High Fidelity**: Files and dataInjections represent actual package contents with high confidence
2. **Practical Coverage**: These mechanisms handle ~90% of real-world non-image artifact distribution
3. **Clear Semantics**: Users understand what's being SBOMed and why
4. **Low False-Positives**: Reduces alert fatigue from build-time dependencies

1. **Phase 1**: Generate SBOMs for all `files` and `dataInjections` components
2. **Phase 2**: Document escape hatches:
   - Custom scripts via hooks that can run additional Syft analysis
   - Clear guidance on identifying and SBOMing git-repo artifacts post-extraction
3. **Phase 3**: Monitor feedback; consider graduated flexibility if patterns emerge

## Tradeoffs Accepted

- **Limitation**: Git repository contents won't be automatically SBOMed (mitigated by documentation)
- **Benefit**: Maintainable, focused, low-noise implementation that covers the most common cases

## Success Criteria

- SBOM includes all files/dataInjections artifacts
- Zero increase in false-positive vulnerability alerts vs. image-only SBOMs
- User feedback indicates the coverage meets 80%+ of use cases

# Architectural Decision Record: Declarative Zarf Package Deployment in Connected Environments

## Status
Proposed

## Context
Zarf was originally designed for disconnected environment deployments with declarative K8s configuration. The requirement for a Zarf init package (which handles cluster initialization, image registry setup, and other foundational components) made sense in disconnected scenarios but creates unnecessary overhead in connected environments where infrastructure already exists.

In connected environments, users want to leverage Zarf's declarative deployment capabilities and package management without the initialization burden, streamlining workflows for organizations with existing cloud infrastructure.

## Decision
Implement an optional declarative deployment path that bypasses the Zarf init package requirement in connected environments, while maintaining init package functionality as the default for disconnected deployments.

## Rationale
1. **Broader Applicability**: Extends Zarf beyond disconnected use cases, making it viable for connected environment deployments
2. **Reduced Complexity**: Eliminates unnecessary initialization steps in scenarios where infrastructure is already provisioned
3. **Backwards Compatibility**: Preserves existing init package workflows; this is additive, not replacing
4. **User Choice**: Allows teams to opt into simplified workflows without disrupting current implementations

## Consequences

### Positive
- Increased adoption in connected environments
- Simplified deployment workflows for users with pre-existing infrastructure
- Better support for GitOps and CI/CD integration patterns

### Negative
- Additional code paths to maintain and test
- Potential for misconfiguration if users skip necessary initialization steps
- Documentation must clearly distinguish between connected and disconnected workflows

## Implementation Considerations
- Add configuration flags to skip init package requirement
- Provide validation to ensure minimum prerequisites are met
- Create separate documentation paths for connected vs. disconnected deployments
- Maintain clear warnings about prerequisites when init is skipped

There has been a long-standing usability gap with Zarf when doing local development due to a lack of local image support. A solution was merged in, [#1173](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/pull/1173), and released in [v0.23.4](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/releases/tag/v0.23.4) to support this feature. Unfortunately, some of the methods that did work well were up to 3 times slower than the current implementation, though they avoided the OOM issue. Lastly, the docker daemon save operations directly still ended up being slower than crane and docker produced a legacy format that would cause issues with [future package schema changes](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/issues/1319) we are planning for oci imports.

# Architectural Decision Record: Local Docker Image Loading Strategy

## Decision

Continue using Crane as the primary method for loading local Docker images into Zarf packages, while implementing the following mitigation strategies for OOM issues:

1. **Default to Crane's memory-efficient mode** for large images, accepting the performance tradeoff
2. **Implement configurable thresholds** allowing users to specify image size limits
3. **Add user documentation and warnings** about memory requirements for large images
4. **Provide explicit configuration options** to select alternative loading strategies when needed

## Rationale

### Why Crane Despite OOM Risk

- **Performance superiority**: Crane is 1.5-3x faster than alternative implementations across all tested scenarios
- **Future compatibility**: Crane produces OCI-compliant output, ensuring alignment with planned schema changes (Issue #1319)
- **Consistency**: Maintains a single, well-tested code path rather than multiple implementations

### Why Not Alternatives

- **Docker CLI**: 2-3x slower than Crane; produces legacy format incompatible with future OCI imports
- **Skopeo/Docker Go Client**: Comparable or slower performance without OOM advantages
- **Multiple implementations**: Increases maintenance burden and testing complexity

### Addressing the OOM Issue

Rather than replacing Crane entirely, the OOM problem is more effectively addressed through:

1. **User agency**: Document memory requirements; let operators choose performance vs. safety tradeoffs
2. **Progressive enhancement**: Implement opt-in memory-safe mode via configuration flags
3. **Monitoring**: Add warnings when available system memory is insufficient

## Consequences

### Positive
- Maintains optimal performance for typical use cases
- Ensures long-term package format compatibility
- Simplifies codebase maintenance

### Negative
- OOM risk remains for very large images on memory-constrained systems
- Requires clear documentation to prevent user surprises
- May necessitate operational guidance for enterprise deployments

## Status
**Accepted** - Implement with documented caveats and user-configurable alternatives

# ADR: Flux Pre-Installation and Selective Big Bang Image/Repository Inclusion in Zarf Packages

## Status
Proposed

## Context

Zarf users deploying Big Bang face significant challenges:

1. **Flux Dependency**: Big Bang requires Flux to be pre-installed for CRD compatibility
2. **Image Bloat**: Big Bang's image manifest (10s of GB) contains a superset of images needed for typical deployments
3. **Repository Superset**: Git repositories defined in Big Bang exceed what most deployments require
4. **Dynamic Discovery**: The specific images needed depend on deployment-specific `values.yaml` configuration, making static packaging inefficient
5. **Values Injection Complexity**: Integrating custom `values.yaml` into Big Bang's kustomization structure is non-trivial

## Decision

Zarf will implement a **selective packaging strategy for Big Bang deployments** with the following components:

1. **Flux Pre-Installation**: Bundle and auto-deploy Flux v2 as a required initialization step before Big Bang package deployment
2. **Values-Driven Image Selection**: Provide tooling to analyze a deployment-specific `values.yaml` file and determine only the required images/repositories
3. **Package Templating**: Support template-based Zarf package definitions that reference the analyzed image/repository subset
4. **Values Integration Layer**: Create a Zarf component that properly injects custom `values.yaml` into Big Bang's kustomization structure
5. **Optional Module Support**: Allow Big Bang modules to be selectively included/excluded at package creation time

## Rationale

- **Reduces Package Size**: Only including necessary images/repos dramatically decreases storage requirements
- **Improves User Experience**: Eliminates manual Flux installation and values discovery steps
- **Maintains Flexibility**: Supports varying deployment configurations without monolithic packages
- **Aligns with Zarf Philosophy**: Enables declarative, reproducible deployments of complex applications

## Consequences

**Positive:**
- Smaller, more deployable packages
- Faster package creation and transfer times
- Clearer dependency management
- Better user onboarding

**Negative:**
- Increased tooling complexity
- Requires documentation of Big Bang's dependency model
- Package generation requires Big Bang knowledge/tooling
- Need to maintain compatibility with Big Bang versions

# Architectural Decision Record: OCI Registry-Based Package Distribution for Zarf

## Decision

We will implement native support for publishing and distributing Zarf packages through OCI-compliant registries, with integrated cryptographic signing capabilities to ensure package integrity and supply chain security.

## Rationale

### Address Current Limitations
The existing local-only and manual transfer distribution model does not scale for widespread adoption. OCI registries provide:
- **Standardized infrastructure** that organizations already operate and trust
- **Global accessibility** without custom hosting requirements
- **Built-in versioning and metadata management**

### Security-First Approach
By making signing a first-class feature alongside publishing:
- Package creators establish **cryptographic provenance** for their packages
- Deployers can **verify authenticity** before installation, preventing tampering
- The solution addresses supply chain security concerns from the outset rather than as an afterthought

### Alignment with Ecosystem Standards
OCI compliance ensures:
- **Interoperability** with existing container registries (Docker Hub, Harbor, Artifactory, etc.)
- **Familiar operational model** for teams already managing container images
- **Leverage of existing registry infrastructure** rather than requiring custom solutions

## Implementation Strategy

1. **OCI Publishing Layer**: Extend Zarf CLI to support pushing packages to OCI registries
2. **Signing Integration**: Implement cryptographic signing (using industry standards like Cosign or similar)
3. **Verification Mechanism**: Enable deployers to validate package signatures before deployment
4. **Registry Metadata**: Store package metadata using OCI annotations for discoverability

## Consequences

**Positive:**
- Dramatically improves package distribution scalability
- Establishes trust and security as core distribution features
- Reduces operational complexity by reusing existing infrastructure
- Enables public and private package sharing models

**Risks to Mitigate:**
- Requires additional authentication and credential management
- Need to establish signing key management best practices documentation
- Registry access dependencies on external services

# Architectural Decision Record: Expanding Zarf's Artifact and Package Management Capabilities

## Status
Proposed

## Context

Zarf currently provides airgap support primarily through:
- Git servers (limited to Flux `GitRepository` objects)
- Container registries

1. **Development workflows**: Lacks support for language-specific package managers and build dependencies (npm, pip, maven, go modules, etc.)

   - Support custom handlers for organization-specific artifact sources

- **Broader airgap support**: Enables Zarf to serve as a comprehensive solution for both production deployments and development environments
- **Developer productivity**: Reduces friction for developers working in disconnected environments
- **Native tooling compatibility**: Allows developers to use familiar package managers and git workflows without significant process changes

# Architectural Decision Record: Zarf v1.0 Release Readiness

## Status
Proposed

## Context
Zarf currently operates as a pre-release product with frequent breaking changes and incomplete test coverage. While it functions in mission-critical environments, it requires deep Zarf expertise to operate successfully. To achieve "Generally Available" v1.x.x status, Zarf must transition to a product that non-expert users can reliably deploy in critical operations without requiring specialized Zarf knowledge.

## Decision
Establish a formal release readiness framework with the following commitments for v1.0 and beyond:

1. **API Stability**: Implement semantic versioning with a stability guarantee for v1.x.x APIs. Any breaking changes require major version bumps and documented migration paths.

2. **Test Coverage Requirements**: Establish minimum thresholds for:
   - Unit test coverage (target: >80%)
   - Integration test coverage for mission-critical paths
   - End-to-end testing across supported deployment environments

3. **Documentation and Usability**: Provide comprehensive user-facing documentation with clear abstractions, so operators without Zarf expertise can successfully deploy and manage systems.

4. **Backwards Compatibility**: Freeze the public API and configuration formats at v1.0, with deprecation periods for any necessary changes in subsequent v1.x releases.

5. **Release Process**: Establish clear versioning and release cadence with beta/RC periods for community validation before GA releases.

## Consequences
- **Positive**: Enables mission-critical adoption; builds user trust; reduces operational friction
- **Negative**: Constrains development velocity; requires significant testing infrastructure investment; demands rigorous API design before v1.0

## Context

The idea of `hooks` is to provide a way for cluster maintainers to register functionality that runs during the deployment lifecycle. Zarf packages already have the concept of `actions` that can execute commands on the host machine's shell during certain package lifecycle events. As `actions` gain more adoption, the team has noticed they are being used to add functionality to Zarf in unexpected ways. We want `actions` to be a tool that extends upon the functionality of Zarf and its packages, not a tool that works around missing or clunky functionality.

We want package creators to be able to create system agnostic packages by leveraging core Zarf functionality. The following is one such scenario:

- _IF_ ECR is chosen as the external registry during `zarf init` / cluster creation, _THEN_ Zarf will seamlessly leverage ECR without requiring advanced user effort.

Using ECR as a remote registry creates 2 problems that Zarf will need to solve:

 1. ECR authentication tokens expire after 12 hours and need to be refreshed. This means the cluster will need to constantly be refreshing its tokens and the user deploying packages will need to make sure they have a valid token.
 2. ECR Image Repositories do not support 'push-to-create'. This means we will need to explicitly create an image repository for every image that is being pushed within the Zarf package.

Packages that get deployed onto a cluster initialized with ECR as its remote registry will need to make sure it solves these 2 problems.

Currently there are 2 solutions:

1. The package deployer solves the problem pre-deployment (creating needed repos, secrets, etc...)
2. The package itself solves these problems with `actions` that are custom built for ECR clusters.

Neither one of these current solutions are ideal. We don't want to require overly complex external + prior actions for Zarf package deployments, and we don't want package creators to have to create and distribute packages that are specific to ECR.

# Architectural Decision Record: Hook System for Registry-Agnostic Package Deployments

## Decision

Implement a **hooks system** that allows Zarf core to register and execute lifecycle callbacks during package deployment, enabling automatic handling of registry-specific requirements (authentication, repository creation, etc.) without requiring package creators to build registry-specific logic into their packages via `actions`.

## Rationale

### Problems with Current Approaches

1. **Pre-deployment burden**: Requiring deployers to manually handle ECR setup (token refresh, repo creation) violates the principle of seamless integration and creates operational friction
2. **Package duplication**: Creating registry-specific package variants defeats the purpose of system-agnostic packages and creates maintenance burden
3. **Action abuse**: Using `actions` as a workaround for missing Zarf functionality couples package logic to infrastructure concerns

### Why Hooks Solve This

- **Separation of Concerns**: Registry-specific logic lives in Zarf core (hooks), not in packages
- **Automatic Execution**: Hooks execute transparently during known lifecycle events without package creator involvement
- **Reusability**: A single ECR hook handles all packages deployed on ECR-initialized clusters
- **Extensibility**: Zarf core can implement hooks for any registry provider without package changes

## Implementation Direction

The hooks system should:

1. **Allow Zarf core** to register handlers for package lifecycle events (pre-image-push, pre-deployment, post-deployment, etc.)
2. **Execute automatically** based on initialized registry type (detected from `zarf-state.yaml`)
3. **Handle registry-specific operations**:
   - Token refresh for ECR
   - Repository pre-creation for ECR
   - Similar patterns for other registries (Azure ACR, GCP Artifact Registry, etc.)
4. **Remain invisible to packages** — no package configuration needed

## Trade-offs

| Aspect | Benefit | Cost |
|--------|---------|------|
| **Zarf Complexity** | Cleaner packages | More core logic |
| **Operational Burden** | Lower for deployers | Requires Zarf updates for new registries |
| **Package Portability** | Fully registry-agnostic | N/A |

## Next Steps

1. Define hook interface and lifecycle events
2. Implement ECR-specific hooks as proof-of-concept
3. Document for package creators and maintainers

# Architectural Decision Record: Zarf Transformation Decoupling Strategy

## Decision

**Use gRPC to decouple Zarf transformations and enable TypeScript/Go synchronization.**

## Rationale

### Why gRPC Over Alternatives

**vs. WASM:**
- WASM would require compiling Go to WebAssembly, introducing complexity and potential performance overhead
- Loses the ability to leverage the hardened Go implementation directly
- Still requires synchronization logic between implementations

**vs. REST:**
- gRPC provides stronger type safety through Protocol Buffers, reducing synchronization errors
- Better performance for frequent transformation calls (binary protocol vs. JSON)
- Streaming capabilities for bulk transformations if needed
- More efficient for service-to-service communication in Kubernetes environments

**vs. Rewrite in TypeScript:**
- Directly contradicts the goal of leveraging battle-tested, hardened Go code
- Introduces maintenance burden and duplication risk
- Requires re-hardening and security audits of new code
- Unnecessary engineering effort

### Benefits of Selected Approach

1. **Single Source of Truth:** Go library remains canonical; TypeScript calls it via gRPC
2. **Reliability:** Continues using proven Zarf transformation logic
3. **Performance:** Binary protocol with minimal serialization overhead
4. **Type Safety:** Protocol Buffers enforce contract consistency
5. **Maintainability:** No code duplication between Go and TypeScript
6. **Kubernetes Native:** Natural fit for pod-to-pod communication

## Implementation Considerations

- Define `.proto` files for transformation operations
- Create gRPC server within Zarf or as sidecar
- Generate TypeScript client from protobuf definitions
- Establish service versioning strategy
- Plan for graceful degradation if service unavailable

**Proposed** (awaiting team review and approval)

# Architectural Decision Record: Zarf Component Composition Refactoring

## Status
Proposed

## Context

Zarf's component composition feature (introduced in v0.16.0) enables package creators to build complex packages from reusable components. However, several architectural issues have emerged as the feature scaled:

1. **Import Chain Scalability**: The current implementation doesn't handle deep import chains well, with test coverage limited to single-level imports
2. **OCI Skeleton Integration**: OCI skeletons were added incrementally without reconsidering their impact on the overall composition model
3. **Component Filtering Fragmentation**: The `only` filter lacks centralized implementation, causing bugs and inconsistent behavior across create-time operations

## Decision

**Refactor the component composition system with the following approach:**

1. **Centralize Import Chain Resolution**
   - Implement a unified import resolver that handles arbitrary nesting depth
   - Add comprehensive test coverage for multi-level import chains
   - Build dependency graph validation to detect cycles and conflicts early

2. **Integrate OCI Skeletons as First-Class Citizens**
   - Re-architect OCI skeleton handling as part of the core composition model rather than as a bolt-on feature
   - Ensure skeleton resolution works seamlessly within import chains
   - Define clear interaction rules between traditional imports and OCI-based composition

3. **Implement Centralized Component Filtering**
   - Create a single filtering mechanism for the `only` filter
   - Apply this filter consistently at the composition layer
   - Remove distributed filtering logic from individual operations

## Rationale

- **Scalability**: Centralized resolution handles arbitrary complexity systematically
- **Maintainability**: Single source of truth for composition rules reduces bugs
- **Consistency**: Unified filtering ensures predictable behavior across all create-time operations
- **Future-proofing**: Architectural clarity enables easier feature additions

## Consequences

- **Positive**: Improved reliability, clearer codebase, better testability
- **Negative**: Requires significant refactoring; potential temporary API disruption during transition
- **Effort**: Substantial engineering investment required

## Context

> Feature request: <https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/issues/2169>

The current package development lifecycle is:

1. Create a `zarf.yaml` file and add components
2. Create a package with `zarf package create <dir>`
3. Debug any create errors and resolve by editing `zarf.yaml` and repeating step 2
4. Run `zarf init` to initialize the cluster
5. Deploy the package with `zarf package deploy <tarball>`
6. Debug any deploy errors and resolve by editing `zarf.yaml` and repeating step 2 or 5

If there are deployment errors, the common pattern is to reset the cluster (ex: `k3d cluster delete && k3d cluster create`) and repeat steps 4-6. Re-initializing the cluster, recreating the package, and redeploying the package is tedious and time consuming; especially when the package is large or the change was small.

`zarf package create` is designed around air-gapped environments where the package is created in one environment and deployed in another. Due to this architecture, a package's dependencies _must_ be retrieved and assembled _each_ and _every_ time.

There already exists the concept of [`YOLO` mode](0010-yolo-mode.md), which can build + deploy a package without the need for `zarf init`, and builds without fetching certain heavy dependencies (like Docker images). However, `YOLO` mode is not exposed via CLI flags, and is meant to develop and deploy packages in fully connected environments.

# ADR: Expose YOLO Mode for Faster Development Iteration

## Status
Proposed

## Context

The current package development workflow requires repeated, time-consuming cycles of:
- Editing `zarf.yaml`
- Recreating the entire package (`zarf package create`)
- Resetting the cluster
- Reinitializing and redeploying

This is particularly inefficient for:
- Large packages (long build times)
- Small iterative changes
- Rapid debugging cycles

While `YOLO` mode already exists internally and supports building + deploying without full dependency fetching and without requiring `zarf init`, it is:
- Not exposed via CLI flags
- Undocumented as a development tool
- Only suitable for fully-connected environments (opposite of the air-gapped design philosophy)

## Decision

**Expose YOLO mode as a CLI flag option** to enable faster development iteration cycles while maintaining the integrity of production air-gapped workflows.

### Specific Actions:
1. Add `--yolo` flag to `zarf package create` command
2. Add `--yolo` flag to `zarf package deploy` command
3. Document YOLO mode as a **development-only** workflow for fully-connected environments
4. Ensure YOLO mode skips heavy dependency fetching (Docker images, registries, etc.)
5. Make YOLO deployments independent of `zarf init` when applicable
6. Add clear warnings that YOLO packages are not suitable for air-gapped deployments

## Rationale

- **Reduces friction** in the development workflow without changing core architecture
- **Reuses existing capability** rather than building new functionality
- **Maintains separation of concerns**: YOLO for development (connected), standard mode for production (air-gapped)
- **Lowers barrier to entry** for package developers iterating locally
- **Minimal risk**: YOLO mode is already functional; we're just exposing it

## Consequences

### Positive
- Significant reduction in development iteration time
- Lower cognitive load on developers during debugging
- Better developer experience for local testing

### Negative
- Risk of YOLO packages being mistakenly used in air-gapped deployments if not properly warned
- Additional CLI surface area to maintain and document
- Potential confusion between YOLO and standard deployment workflows

### Mitigation
- Strong documentation and clear CLI help text warning against air-gapped use
- Error messaging if YOLO packages are deployed without proper cluster connectivity
- Training/onboarding materials distinguishing development vs. production workflows

## Alternatives Considered

1. **Build a new "dev mode"**: Duplicates YOLO functionality; rejected in favor of reuse
2. **Require manual cluster reset**: Status quo; unacceptably slow for iterative development
3. **Auto-detect connectivity**: Complexity added; explicit flag is clearer

# Architectural Decision Record

## Title
Migration Strategy for Documentation Platform

## Status
Pending Decision

## Context
The current documentation site is built with Docusaurus 2. While Docusaurus has served us well, it has some limitations, primarily around performance and dependency management.

## Decision

**Conduct a comprehensive evaluation of documentation platforms before making a migration decision.**

### Recommended Approach:

1. **Evaluate Alternative Platforms**
   - Assess VitePress, Astro, Nextra, or static site generators
   - Compare on: build performance, bundle size, dependency footprint, maintenance burden
   - Benchmark against current Docusaurus setup

2. **Quantify Current Pain Points**
   - Document specific performance metrics (build time, page load times)
   - Identify dependency management issues with concrete examples
   - Assess maintenance cost vs. benefit of migration

3. **Assess Migration Effort**
   - Evaluate content migration complexity
   - Consider plugin/customization dependencies
   - Plan incremental migration if feasible

4. **Decision Criteria**
   - Performance gain threshold (e.g., 40%+ build time reduction)
   - Dependency count reduction target
   - Community support and long-term viability
   - Team learning curve and expertise

## Consequences

**Positive:**
- Potential performance and maintainability improvements
- Reduced technical debt
- Aligned with current industry trends

**Negative:**
- Migration effort required
- Team ramp-up time on new platform
- Temporary documentation process disruption

## Next Steps
- Establish evaluation criteria and timelines
- Run proof-of-concept migration for subset of documentation
- Present findings with migration recommendation

## Context

Zarf is currently using an in-house built logging solution which in turn depends on pterm. This solution is used to output information to the end user who is using the Zarf CLI. This output is for the most part formatted with the purpose of CLI user experience. Logging function calls are done both in the CLI specific code as well as in the packages. The logging is implemented in such a way that different levels exist with different impacts and log destinations. A common pattern that is used is to call `message.Fatal` whenever an error occurs. This will output the message to STDERR while writing the actual error message to a debug log and exiting the program. Exiting the program in this manner makes unit testing difficult while also skipping proper context handling and skipping any clean-up that was intended to run before exiting the program. Some logging components like the progress bar and spinner are accessed through a shared global state that is not thread safe. The coupling to logging becomes complicated as disabling the progress bar is a challenge while multi threading these functions which access the global state resulting in complicated access patterns.

# Architectural Decision Record: Logging System Refactoring

## Status
Proposed

## Context
Zarf's current in-house logging solution presents several architectural problems:

1. **Testing Impediments**: Direct calls to `message.Fatal()` exit the program immediately, preventing proper unit testing and error scenario validation
2. **Control Flow Issues**: Premature program termination bypasses cleanup handlers, defer statements, and context cancellation
3. **Global State**: Progress bars and spinners rely on unsafe shared global state, creating thread-safety issues
4. **Coupling Challenges**: Tight coupling between packages and CLI-specific logging makes components difficult to reuse or test in isolation
5. **Concurrency Problems**: Multi-threaded scenarios require complicated access patterns to manage global state

## Decision

**Adopt a structured logging approach with the following principles:**

1. **Replace Fatal Calls with Error Returns**: Package functions should return errors instead of calling `message.Fatal()`. Let callers decide how to handle errors.

2. **Implement Context-Aware Logging**: Use Go's `context` package to propagate cancellation signals and control flow without forcing exits.

3. **Separate Concerns**: Decouple business logic logging from CLI presentation:
   - Use a standard structured logging library (e.g., `slog`, `zap`, or `logrus`) for packages
   - Retain user-facing formatting in CLI layer only

4. **Remove Global State**: Replace global progress/spinner state with dependency injection:
   - Pass logger/progress interfaces as parameters
   - Make components explicitly testable without global initialization

5. **Gradual Migration Strategy**:
   - Create wrapper interfaces around the logging system
   - Migrate package layer first (return errors, accept logger interface)
   - Update CLI layer to handle errors and decide output formatting
   - Deprecate direct `message.Fatal` calls in packages

## Consequences

### Positive
- ✅ Improved testability with proper error scenarios
- ✅ Proper cleanup via deferred functions and context cancellation
- ✅ Thread-safe concurrent operations
- ✅ Reusable packages independent of CLI concerns
- ✅ Clearer separation between business logic and presentation

### Negative
- ❌ Significant refactoring effort across codebase
- ❌ Temporary increase in error handling verbosity at CLI layer
- ❌ Learning curve for structured logging patterns
- ❌ Potential breaking changes to package APIs

## Implementation Notes
- Start with new code following the pattern
- Gradually migrate critical paths (prioritize high-concurrency components)
- Maintain backwards compatibility layer during transition period
- Add logging integration tests alongside unit tests

## Context

Zarf currently does not have explicit schema versions. Any schema changes are embedded into Zarf and can change with new versions. There are several examples of deprecated keys throughout Zarf's lifespan such as:

- `setVariable` deprecated in favor of `setVariables`
- `scripts` deprecated in favor of `actions`
- `group` deprecated in favor of `flavor`, however these work functionally different and cannot be automatically migrated
- `cosignKeyPath` deprecated in favor of specifying the key path at create time

Zarf has not disabled any deprecated keys thus far. On create the user is always warned when using a deprecated field, however the field still exists in the schema and functions properly. Some of the deprecated keys can be migrated automatically as the old item is a subset or directly related to it's replacement. For example, setVariable is automatically migrated to a single item list of setVariables. This migration occurs on the zarf.yaml fed into the package during package create, however the original field is not deleted from the packaged zarf.yaml because the Zarf binary used in the airgap or delivery environment is not assumed to have the new schema fields that the deprecated key was migrated to.

The release of v1 will provide an opportunity to delete deprecated features that Zarf has warned will be dropped in v1.

Creating a v1 schema will allow Zarf to establish a contract with it's user base that features will be supported long term. When a feature is deprecated in the v1 schema, it will remain usable in the schema for the lifetime of v1.

# Architectural Decision Record: Schema Versioning and Deprecation Policy for Zarf v1

## Decision

Implement explicit schema versioning for Zarf v1 with the following approach:

1. **Introduce explicit schema versioning** starting with v1.0, enabling clear version tracking and migration paths
2. **Remove all deprecated fields** from the v1 schema (setVariable, scripts, group, cosignKeyPath, etc.)
3. **Implement automatic schema migration** that converts deprecated fields to their v1-compliant equivalents during package creation
4. **Establish a v1 stability contract** guaranteeing that any fields in the v1 schema will remain supported throughout the v1 release cycle
5. **Delete migrated deprecated fields** from packaged zarf.yaml files to ensure forward compatibility across different Zarf binary versions

## Rationale

- **Clear user contract**: Explicit versioning signals stability and long-term support commitments
- **Technical debt elimination**: v1 milestone provides a clean break to remove legacy fields accumulated over development
- **Improved maintainability**: Reduces code complexity from supporting multiple deprecated code paths
- **Better interoperability**: Packaged bundles with only v1-compliant fields work reliably across Zarf versions
- **Migration clarity**: Automatic migration with warnings during create-time provides a smooth user transition

## Consequences

**Positive:**
- Users on v1 have guaranteed schema stability
- Easier to maintain and evolve the codebase forward
- Clear deprecation path for future v2+ development

**Negative:**
- Breaking change for users still using deprecated fields (migration required)
- Requires robust migration logic to prevent user disruption
- Documentation burden to guide users through schema updates

## Implementation Notes

- Maintain migration warnings during `zarf package create` to guide users
- Consider tooling or documentation to help users update their zarf.yaml files
- Establish clear deprecation policies for post-v1 releases

## Decision

Zarf will begin having proper schema versions. A top level key, `apiVersion`, will be introduced to allow users to specify the schema. At the release of v1 the only valid user input for `apiVersion` will be v1. Zarf will not allow users to build using the v0 schema. `zarf package create` will fail if the user has deprecated keys or if `apiVersion` is missing and the user will be instructed to run the new `zarf dev migrate-schema` command. `zarf dev migrate-schema` will automatically migrate deprecated fields in the users `zarf.yaml` where possible. It will also add the apiVersion key and set it to v1.

The existing go types which comprise the Zarf schema will be moved to types/alpha and will never change. An updated copy of these types without the deprecated fields will be created in a package types/v1 and any future schema changes will affect these objects. Internally, Zarf will introduce translation functions which will take the alpha schema and return the v1 schema. From that point on, all function signatures that have a struct that is included in the Zarf schema will change from `types.structName` to `v1.structName`.

All deprecated features will cause an error on create. Deprecated features with a direct migration path will still be deployed if the package was created with schema v1, as migrations will add the non deprecated fields. If a feature does not have a direct automatic migration path (cosignKeyPath & groups) the package will fail on deploy. This will happen until the alpha schema is entirely removed from Zarf, which will happen one year after v1 is released.

At create time Zarf will package both a `zarf.yaml` and a `zarfv1.yaml`. If a `zarfv1.yaml` exists Zarf will use that. If a `zarfv1.yaml` does not exist, then Zarf will know that the package was created prior to v1 and use the regular `zarf.yaml`. If the package is deployed with v0 it will read the `zarf.yaml` as normal even if the package has a `zarfv1.yaml`. This will make it simpler to drop deprecated items with migration paths from the v1 schema while remaining backwards compatible as those deprecated items will exist in the `zarf.yaml`

When Zarf introduces new keys that they are not ready to promise long term support for they will mark them as experimental in the schema. A key is assumed to be stable if it's not experimental or deprecated.

There are several other keys Zarf will deprecate which will have automated migrations to new fields
- `.metadata.aggregateChecksum` -> `.build.aggregateChecksum`
- `.components[x].required` -> `.components[x].optional`. Optional will default to false. This is a change in behavior as currently `required` defaults to true. However, automatic migration will work since we can set optional to true on any components which do not already have required.
- Metadata fields `image`, `source`, `documentation`, `url`, `authors`, `vendors` -> will become a map of `annotations`
- `noWait` -> `wait` which will default to true. This change will happen on both `.components.[x].manifests` and `components.[x].charts`
- `yolo` -> `airgap` which will default to true
- `.components.[x].actions.[default/onAny].maxRetries` -> `.components.[x].actions.[default/onAny].retries`
- `.components.[x].actions.[default/onAny].maxTotalSeconds` -> `.components.[x].actions.[default/onAny].timeout`, which must be in a [Go recognized duration string format](https://pkg.go.dev/time#ParseDuration)
- charts will change to avoid [current confusion with keys](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/issues/2245). Exactly one of the following fields will exist for each `components.[x].charts`.
```yaml
  helm:
    url: https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo
    RepoName: podinfo # replaces repoName since it's only applicable for helm repos

  git:
    url: https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo
    path: charts/podinfo

  oci:
    url: oci://ghcr.io/stefanprodan/charts/podinfo

  local:
   path: chart
```
- A new field called `.components.[x].healthChecks` will be introduced and will utilize [kstatus](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cli-utils/blob/master/pkg/kstatus/README.md) to wait for resources to be ready after deployment. Read [#2718](https://github.com/zarf-dev/zarf/issues/2718) for more detail.
- a new field `.components.[x].wait` will be introduced. It will default to true, and automatically run `healthchecks` for every object in the cluster.
- `.components.[x].extensions` will be removed in favor of `zarf dev generate bigbang`. See #2875
